question_type: Ratio-of-ratios of one pinned corpus value converted at external annual-average USD/INR rates; the corpus value cancels algebraically, so the answer depends only on an exchange rate the corpus does not contain (1966 devaluation-year average)
decisive_step: Two decisions, neither settled by the corpus: (1) reading - one pinned Jan-31-1964 survey value converted at three yearly rates (then the value cancels and the answer is |r65/r64 - r66/r65|) versus each year's own Jan-31 survey value at its own rate; (2) the external 1966 annual-average INR/USD rate (the 1964 and 1965 peg years cancel to exactly 1, so the whole 4-dp answer is the 1966 average divided by the pre-devaluation peg, minus 1). The reference chose the single-value reading at worklog.md Step 1 and recalled an IMF/World Bank period average at worklog.md Step 6 (calc.py comment block), and was itself graded wrong; review.md's verdict is 'uncertain' and names the external 1966 rate as the only sensitivity. By the error bins (c within_1pct; a, b 1-5pct; reference wrong), the key is not the recalled period average nor the 2-dp rounding of it: the reference's own rejected alternative reading (worklog Step 7 'Alt reading') and its day-weighted 1966 sensitivity case both fall within about half a percent of c's value, so the key uses one of those two conventions. Which one cannot be settled without the key.

a.path_summary: Found the Jan 31 1964 ownership-survey total on the first find_tables/show_table pair (a[6], a[8]) and stated the cancelling algebra at a[4]. Then spent a[10]-[150] searching the corpus for a rupee/exchange-rate table (find_tables 'exchange rates', 'rupee', 'India', 'IFS', rg over 1960s-70s issues), concluding several times that there is none (a[33], a[49], a[143]). Two degenerate loops: one rg repeated 29 times (a[59]-[116]) and another 57 times (a[165]-[278]), with a Codex-side compaction in between ('Handoff says' at a[131]; events.jsonl warns of 'multiple compactions'). At a[151]-[155] and a[303]-[305] it settled on a month-weighted blend of the pre- and post-devaluation pegs (5 months old, 7 months new) as the 1966 average and computed with calc; 1697 s, 306 steps, 15.8M input tokens.

first_divergence.what_it_did: Took the 1966 annual average as a 5/7 month-weighted blend of the two pegs (it also considered a 2-dp recalled figure at a[155] and picked the blend at a[305]).
first_divergence.what_a_right_cell_or_the_reference_did: No cell was right. The reference recalled an IMF/WB period average at full precision (worklog Step 6) and was also wrong; c, the closest, used a recalled WDI figure that happens to sit near a day-weighted blend (c[78]-[79]). The key appears to follow either a day-weighted 1966 average or the year-specific-survey reading (see decisive_step).

smallest_change.change: Hard loop break with a corpus-exhausted note. Runtime behaviour: when a command's normalized text equals one already run >= 2 times in this episode and the earlier output hash is identical, do NOT execute it; return only: '[harness:loop] not run - identical to call N, whose output is unchanged. Searches for <top query noun> so far: K commands, 0 matching tables (find_tables) / 0 matching lines in <years> (rg). If the corpus has no such table, say so in your notes and continue with the values you have. Candidates: <list or none>.' On the 6th identical command, additionally require a checkpoint: the next call must be either a command never run before or submit --answer. Apply in all cells (a had no guard at all and repeated one rg 57 times; b's note-only guard was ignored 30 times).
smallest_change.could_hurt_right_cells: unlikely - it only triggers on byte-identical commands with byte-identical output, which carry no new information; right cells on ordinal 28 never repeated a command more than twice
smallest_change.confidence: high for cost (a: 1697 s -> well under 500 s; b: 834 s -> ~300 s), none for correctness: the answer is irreducible (see irreducible)

alternatives.change: Add to AGENTS.md: 'Some questions need a public figure the corpus does not contain (an exchange rate, a price index, a population). After one targeted pass - find_tables with the key noun and rg -i for it over the relevant years - shows nothing, write in your notes that the value is external, use the standard published annual series (IMF/World Bank period average) at full precision, name it in your notes, and go on. Do not keep searching.'
alternatives.why_not_first: It shortens the search phase (all three cells wrote 'but task says local references' and kept looking: a[143], a[149], b[60], c[49]) but cannot stop the degenerate repetition, which began after the model had already concluded there was no table (a[33] -> loop from a[59]); and it cannot make the recalled figure match the key - a, b, c and the reference all recalled different numbers.

alternatives.change: Gated external-series lookup (only if v10 allows it): 'lookup_series --series USD/INR --stat annual_average --years 1964-1966' backed by a vetted offline table (IMF IFS / WB WDI official rate, period average) that prints value, source and vintage, so the number in calc is one a tool output showed and the 'grounded' gate can bind it.
alternatives.why_not_first: Changes the benchmark's closed-corpus premise; and the key's convention here does not match the standard period average, so even this would not have made the cell right.

fix.why_not_text: Cell a had the 'Loops' sentence and still repeated one rg 29 times and another 57 times; cell b received seven runtime loop notes and repeated the same query 33 times. Repetition here is a degenerate model state (identical THINK/SAY/RUN triples), which only a runtime refusal to re-execute can break. For the answer itself no text can help: the deciding number is outside the corpus and the reference, with a careful recall and sensitivity analysis, got it wrong too.
fix.irreducible: Yes for correctness. The answer is determined entirely by an external exchange-rate convention (and possibly by a reading choice the question leaves ambiguous); the reference solver flagged its own answer 'uncertain' for exactly this reason and was graded wrong. No adapter change can make a closed-corpus run hit a 4-dp figure that depends on which published 1966 average (or which base-value reading) the key used. What is reducible is the cost: a and b spent >80% of their steps in loops.

notes: 1) The b gate's 'table_alternatives' rule bound 'used_ref' to a bond-yield line the model had merely read, then recommended TSO-2 of a 1969 issue for a question pinned to Jan 31 1964 - a false positive that cost 4 steps; the rule should only fire on lines the calc inputs actually came from. 2) The 'grounded' rule worked as designed on the external peg literal, and the keep path is the right outcome for external inputs; v10 could let the model declare an input external ('--external "<source>"') so the finding is answered rather than kept. 3) The compaction ledger splice (b call 77) showed 20 rows of a 1940s foreign-holdings table because they were the last thing read; a splice keyed to the question's nouns would have been more useful. 4) The corpus's only 'rupee' hits are 1946-54 holdings rows and 1974-81 settlement footnotes (reference worklog Step 4), so 'India' searches lure the model into irrelevant tables (b[218]-[219], c[58]). 5) Cell a's 306 steps include a Codex-client compaction not counted by the harness ('compactions=None'); the 'Handoff says' notes at a[131]/[155] show the actor reasoning from a summary, and the loops start right after those resets. 6) c computed the day-weighted 1966 blends at c[78] and discarded them for a recalled figure at c[79]; had it kept its own computation it would have been at least as close, which is an argument for the TEXT alternative's 'derive, do not recall' wording if v10 keeps closed-corpus rules.
